mid_tier2_why: These two are the same codec generation and it shows: VP9 is only 4.8% ahead at VMAF 90, averaged over the three resolutions, and it never gets further than 7.6 percentage points ahead anywhere. Pick on reach, not on efficiency. VP9 plays in every browser and costs nothing to licence; HEVC does neither, and has hardware everywhere.
vp9_high_why: At this density the two tier-2 codecs are close enough that efficiency stops deciding: VP9 is 3.4% smaller than HEVC at VMAF 95, and both are well behind AV1. So pick on where the file has to play. HEVC is what broadcast chains, UHD Blu-ray, Apple devices and cameras speak natively; VP9 is what browsers speak. If it is going to a television, that is HEVC.
low_tier2_why: Where AV1 is not an option, this is the next best thing when bits are scarce: 16.6% smaller than H.264 at VMAF 80, against 9.8% smaller for the other one. VP9 carries no licence bill and plays in every browser, which is why it takes this square even when the margin over HEVC is small.
converge_note: the best saving against H.264 falls from 32.6% at VMAF 80 to 18.1% at VMAF 95, and the gap between the three non-H.264 codecs closes from 22.8 to 15.8 percentage points
ranking_note: The ordering at VMAF 90 is AV1 then VP9 then HEVC then H.264, and it is that same ordering at every resolution and every target measured bar a few. The exception is one swap: AV1 then VP9 then H.264 then HEVC at 720p VMAF 95, 540p VMAF 95, 540p VMAF 93, 540p VMAF 90. The margins are another matter. AV1 is 27.9% under H.264 at 1080p and 19.2% at 540p; HEVC is 11.1% and -0.8%. The largest swing across resolutions for one codec at one target is 14.4 percentage points (HEVC). Resolution does not reorder the codecs; it decides how much the newer ones are worth, and it points the same way as bitrate does.
claim_hypothesis: Half right, and the half that is right is more useful than it looks. The ranking does not move much: AV1 then VP9 then HEVC then H.264 at 1080p, and the same order almost everywhere else, so HEVC does not win at 1080p between 1 and 10 Mbit/s. AV1 does, by 27.9% against H.264 where HEVC manages 11.1%. But the intuition that resolution matters is correct, just not in the way the question assumed: it changes the size of the win, not its owner. AV1's lead over H.264 goes from 19.2% at 540p to 27.9% at 1080p, and HEVC's from -0.8% to 11.1%: at 540p HEVC is barely worth the trouble. Extrapolate the trend and 4K is where the modern codecs are furthest ahead, for two reasons at once. More pixels gives their larger transforms and prediction blocks more to work with, and 4K at a normal streaming bitrate sits further left on the bits-per-pixel axis, where their lead is largest anyway. 4K60 at 15 Mbit/s is 0.0301 bits per pixel per frame; 1080p30 at 3 Mbit/s is 0.0482.
collapse_note: Three curves, one shape, and a real offset between them. At 0.04 bits per pixel per frame AV1 reaches VMAF 85.5 at 1080p and 78.4 at 540p, a gap of 7.2 points for the same bits per pixel. Higher resolution is cheaper per pixel, because neighbouring pixels are more alike and prediction has more to work with. So normalising by pixel rate puts the resolutions on one axis, not on one line, and what it buys is that the ordering of the codecs and the shape of every curve become directly comparable across them.
cost_note: At matched VMAF 93 and 1080p, AV1 costs 6.8 times what H.264 costs to encode, and HEVC 1.9 times, and VP9 3.9 times. Two things follow. For anything watched once, the encode can easily cost more than the bandwidth it saves. For anything watched a million times, it is free. That, and not compression efficiency, is why live streaming still ships H.264 while catalogue video has moved on.
metric_note: The three metrics disagree, as they always do: at VMAF 90 the largest gap between VMAF's verdict and another metric's is 26.0 percentage points (VP9 scored with SSIM), and the ordering is not identical under all three, so the table is the honest summary and the headline percentages should be read as VMAF's opinion. SSIM is a poor cross-codec judge at low rates and that is where most of the disagreement sits. VMAF's own weaknesses run the other way: it over-rewards sharpening and is weak on banding.
claim_hevc50: Not on these measurements, and not close. Against x264 at the same preset and the same VMAF, x265 came in 11.1% smaller at 1080p and VMAF 90; its best showing anywhere was 18.1% smaller at 1080p and VMAF 80; and at 540p it was 0.8% larger than x264 for the same picture. The 50% figure traces back to Ohm, Sullivan, Tan and Wiegand's 2012 comparison, which measured the HEVC and H.264 reference encoders under subjective testing. Two things shrink it in practice: x264 is a far better H.264 encoder than the reference software was, and PSNR-driven reference comparisons flatter the newer codec. That second point shows up directly in this sweep: score the identical encodes with PSNR-Y instead of VMAF and x265 comes out 24.6% smaller than x264 rather than 11.1% smaller. A good part of the distance between 50% and what you will actually see is the choice of metric. Twenty to thirty percent is the number to plan with at 1080p, and less than that below it.

v_vp9_class.text: Right about close, wrong about the crossover

claim_vp9: The 'very equal' half is right and it is the important half: across every resolution and every target measured, VP9 and HEVC are within 7.6 percentage points of each other, and at VMAF 90 the gap is 4.8%. There is no crossover on this corpus: VP9 is ahead at both ends, by 7.6% at VMAF 80 and 3.4% at VMAF 95. It is a real edge to VP9 and it is a small one. They are the same codec generation, they were finished within a year of each other, and the reason YouTube ships VP9 is that it is royalty-free and plays in Chrome, not that it compresses better. For scale: AV1 files are 15.0% smaller than VP9 files at VMAF 90 for the same picture. That gap is worth choosing on; four percent is not.
claim_av1: This has it exactly backwards, and it is the most common misconception about AV1. Decoding AV1 is a little more expensive than decoding HEVC and is comfortably within a software decoder on any modern CPU; dav1d decodes 1080p faster than real time on a phone core. Hardware decode is now in every 2023-and-later flagship SoC, most smart TVs, and every GPU from RTX 30, RDNA 2 and Intel Arc onward. It is the encode side that is expensive: on this corpus libaom needed 6.8 times H.264's CPU for the same VMAF, and libaom is the slow reference encoder. The hardware you want for AV1 is on the encoder, and most people never touch that side.
method_corpus: 2 pristine uncompressed clips from the Xiph derf collection: park_joy (high motion, 3 s, 150 frames at 50 fps); blue_sky (flat gradient, 3 s, 75 frames at 25 fps). Each was fetched as raw 1080p y4m and downscaled with Lanczos to 720p and 540p; nothing was ever upscaled. Every clip was swept on its own CRF ladder in four encoders at three resolutions, 177 encodes in total, 1.4 CPU-hours of encoding and 0.5 CPU-hours of scoring.
method_metric: Quality was scored with VMAF (model vmaf_v0.6.1) through ffmpeg's libvmaf filter, with PSNR-Y and SSIM recorded in the same pass. Each codec was swept on its own CRF ladder; the rate at a given VMAF target was found by interpolating that codec's own curve per clip, then taking the geometric mean across clips. CRF ladders are per clip, because a single ladder placed to span VMAF 78 to 98 on the high-motion clip only reaches the top of the range on the easy one, and the comparison at the low end would then be an artefact of the sweep. Rate is always bits per pixel per frame; container overhead is removed, so an IVF frame header is not counted against VP9 and AV1. Encoders: ffmpeg 7.0.2 static, libx264, libx265, libvpx-vp9 and libaom-av1, each pinned to a single thread so encoder CPU time is a clean cost measure. The machine was shared with other jobs, which stretches wall-clock time but leaves the CPU-time ratios between codecs intact.
caveat_presets: x264 and x265 ran at -preset medium, VP9 at -cpu-used 2, libaom-AV1 at -cpu-used 6. Slower presets are worth several percent of BD-rate and they are worth most to HEVC and AV1, which have the largest search spaces, so these settings understate HEVC's and AV1's lead rather than overstate it. For scale: a calibration probe at -cpu-used 5 produced a file 12% smaller than -cpu-used 6 at the same CRF on the high-motion clip. That pair was not quality-scored, so read it as an indication of the size of the preset effect rather than as a BD-rate.
caveat_vmaf: VMAF was trained on Netflix's own catalogue and its own scaling pipeline. It over-rewards sharpening and contrast enhancement, it is weak on banding, and it was fitted for 1080p viewed at a set distance. PSNR-Y and SSIM are recorded alongside every encode in the raw data, and the cross-check above shows they do not simply agree: PSNR-Y is markedly more generous to the newer codecs than VMAF is, SSIM markedly less. Where a page quotes one number, it is quoting one metric's opinion. Everything here is VMAF's.
caveat_corpus: 2 clips is a small corpus, and it is deliberately a hard one: the high-motion clip is close to the worst case for any codec, and the flat-gradient clip is the banding worst case. Real catalogue content is easier than both, so the absolute bits-per-pixel numbers here are pessimistic. The compute budget for this environment was shared with other work and libaom is very slow, which is why the corpus is this size; a third clip was fetched and is in the repository, but only partially swept (in_to_tree), so it is excluded from every number on this page rather than half-counted. The direction of every finding is robust to corpus size; the exact percentages are not general constants.
crf_note: Those are ranges because content difficulty moves CRF a long way. On this corpus the high-motion clip and the flat-gradient clip needed x264 CRF 25 and 32 respectively to land on the same VMAF 93: the same setting is a different picture on different footage, which is why per-title encoding exists.
